title: Shuffle until it's sorted
hook: Shuffle 5 cards and stop when they land in order. How long can that take?

knows: n cards can be put in order n! ways (route-explosion)
doesNotKnow: that "shuffle and check" needs about n! tries on average, so 10 cards take millions

misconception: A randomised sort that checks itself will finish in a handful of tries.
objective: The learner can explain that each random shuffle of n distinct cards is in order with probability 1/n!, so shuffle-and-check waits about n! shuffles on average: about 120 for 5 cards, 6 for 3, 24 for 4 and 3.6 million for 10.

claims.text: Seeded runs on this stage: one 5-card run took 183 shuffles, and 100 runs averaged 113 (from 2 to 695). For 3 cards: one run 12, average 7; for 4 cards: one run 43, average 22.
claims.source: Demo.tsx perm() and average(); builder's node script (2026-10-14) with the same mulberry32 and Fisher-Yates of 1..n. Seeds: mulberry32(42 + n) for the single-run stream (hand shuffles and 'Shuffle until sorted' share it, so the run length does not depend on press order), mulberry32(4200 + n) for the 100 runs, mulberry32(7 + n) for the first deal. Seeds follow the spec's scheme and were not chosen for the result. Averages of 100: 6.64, 22.08, 112.76 (shown rounded); longest 5-card run 695. Across 200 other seeds the 5-card average of 100 ranged 89 to 160, so 113 is one example, not the mean. Single runs capped at 5,000 shuffles (never hit by these seeds).

claims.text: Five cards can be ordered 5! = 120 ways, and each shuffle is equally likely to give any of them, so one shuffle in 120 comes out sorted and you wait about 120 shuffles on average.
claims.source: A Fisher-Yates shuffle gives each of the n! orders of n distinct cards probability 1/n! (Knuth, TAOCP vol. 2, Algorithm 3.4.2P). Independent shuffles until the first success are a geometric waiting time with p = 1/n!, whose mean is 1/p = n!. 5! = 120.

claims.text: 3 cards average about 3! = 6 shuffles and 4 cards about 4! = 24.
claims.source: Same geometric argument as c2 with n = 3 and n = 4; 3! = 6, 4! = 24 (arithmetic).

claims.text: Each extra card multiplies the wait. With 10 cards there are 3,628,800 orders, so about 3.6 million shuffles.
claims.source: n! = n x (n - 1)!, so adding the n-th card multiplies the expected wait by n. 10! = 3,628,800 (arithmetic); expected wait 10! by c2.

claims.text: Only one order of the cards counts as sorted; a row with two or three cards in their right place is no closer to done.
claims.source: With distinct cards exactly one of the n! orders is ascending. Each shuffle here reshuffles all the cards from scratch (Fisher-Yates of 1..n, independent of the previous row), so ticks on one row do not change the chance for the next.

claims.text: Shuffling and checking cannot beat n!.
claims.source: Any sort that only shuffles uniformly at random and checks has expected n! shuffles (c2); counting the n - 1 comparisons of each check, bogosort's expected time is Theta(n x n!). Gruber, Holzer and Ruepp, 'Sorting the slow way: an analysis of perversely awful randomized sorting algorithms', FUN 2007 (check before citing).

recall.question: A program shuffles 4 different cards at random and checks each time whether they are in order. About how many shuffles does it need on average?
recall.why: 4 cards have 4! = 24 orders and only one is sorted, so each shuffle has a 1 in 24 chance: on average you wait about 24 shuffles.
